events.title: Ageing Badly
events.description: ‘Ageing Badly’ challenges assumptions that the goal of one’s later years is to age well or ‘successfully’, a message that, since the 1960s, has become pervasive, naturalised in medicine, social theory, and popular culture. Ageing badly, by contrast, encompasses a range of uncomfortable and idiosyncratic ways in which art works, bodies, artists, and ideas, such as ‘the 1960s’, have aged over time. The language of ageing is deeply entangled with those concerning time, history, and the body—languages that have in turn shaped the field of art history and feminist interventions in the field.

events.description: Joshua Aduol will present his FPO "Integrating Physical Structure into Machine Learning: PDE Constraints and Differentiable Dynamics" on Monday, August 31, 2026 at 10:00 AM in CS 401 & Zoom.Zoom Link: https://princeton.zoom.us/j/8051095381The members of Joshua’s committee are as follows:Examiners: Ryan Adams (Adviser), Szymon Rusinkiewicz, Christine Allen-BlanchetteReaders: Ryan Adams (Adviser), Peter Orbanz (University College London)A copy of his thesis is available upon request. Please email gradinfo@cs.princeton.edu if you would like a copy of the thesis.Everyone is invited to attend the talk.Abstract follows below:Despite strong empirical performance, many machine learning models ignore the governing physical laws underlying the data they model. This thesis presents some techniques to address these shortcomings in two complementary directions: 1) enforcing partial differential equations (PDE) constraints in neural networks, and 2) differentiable rigid body dynamics simulation of closed-loop kinematic chains. Within these directions, we present three contributions.In the first project, we develop a method to construct neural networks that output a time-dependent probability density and the corresponding flow field. The approach leverages recent developments in divergence-free neural networks and enables joint modeling without the need of a numerical integrator to compute one from the other. We evaluate it against continuous normalizing flows demonstrating competitive performance with improved computational efficiency.Extending this idea, we then develop a generalization of divergence-free neural networks to enforce underdetermined linear PDE constraints. Using results from PDE theory on the invertibility of linear differential operators, we construct models that satisfy these constraints by design. This yields a flexible framework for PDE-constrained learning problems. We validate the approach against physics-informed neural network baselines demonstrating improved accuracy.Finally, we present a differentiable rigid-body dynamics simulator that natively supports closed-loop mechanisms and enables large-scale vectorized simulation on GPUs. We describe the design principles underlying the system and demonstrate its use in learning controllers for multiple closed-loop mechanisms in parallel, as well as simulating a variety of mechanisms in parallel and comparing it to state-of-the-art differentiable simulators.Together, these contributions advance the integration of physical structure into machine learning models, improving their consistency, efficiency, and applicability to real-world systems.

events.title: CITP Seminar - AI Agents and the Augmentation Agenda
events.description: The dominant paradigm in AI research and development envisions the goal as automation of tasks and entire jobs. But another, comparatively marginalized vision has existed since the beginning of AI — that of augmenting workers and amplifying human potential. In this talk, it is argued that the automation agenda is struggling even on purely commercial grounds, and it is time to invest more into augmentation. Building agents for collaboration instead of automation requires elevating a set of underexplored research challenges in human-computer interaction. Such agents can better serve human flourishing, promote broader economic growth, and put into motion the “pro-worker AI” that economists have advocated for.This talk is based on a collaboration with Gabriel Unger.Bio: Arvind Narayanan is a professor of computer science at Princeton University and the director of the Center for Information Technology Policy. He is a co-author of the bookAI Snake Oiland a newsletter of the same name which is read by 60,000 researchers, policy makers, journalists, and AI enthusiasts. He previously co-authored two widely used computer science textbooks:Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency TechnologiesandFairness in Machine Learning. Narayanan led the Princeton Web Transparency and Accountability Project to uncover how companies collect and use our personal information. His work was among the first to show how machine learning reflects cultural stereotypes. Narayanan was one of TIME’s inaugural list of 100 most influential people in AI. He is a recipient of the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE)This talk will be livestreamed and recorded. The recording will be posted to the CITP website, the CITP YouTube channel and the University Media Central channel.If you need an accommodation for a disability please contact Jean Butcher at butcher@princeton.edu at least one week prior to the event.

events.title: CITP Seminar - DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
events.description: Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work.We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration.Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.”Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations (with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays. He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy, now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review.This talk will be recorded and livestreamed via Zoom. The recording will be posted to the CITP website, the CITP YouTube channel and the University Media Central channel.If you need an accommodation for a disability please contact Jean Butcher at butcher@princeton.edu at least one week prior to the event.

events.title: CITP Seminar - From AI Innovation to AI Deployment: Building the Institutions for an AI-Driven Economy
events.description: Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than the institutions, workforces, and systems expected to absorb it. The challenge ahead is therefore not only one of technological innovation, but of deployment: how do we translate rapidly evolving capabilities into broad-based economic opportunity, institutional capacity, and public benefit?This talk will explore the New Jersey AI Hub as an emerging model for tackling that challenge. A public-private initiative founded by Princeton University, the State of New Jersey, Microsoft, and CoreWeave, the Hub brings together universities, government, industry, startups, and communities to accelerate AI innovation and adoption. Liat Krawczyk will discuss the Hub’s work across entrepreneurship, workforce development, applied AI, and responsible governance—and the larger question underlying it: what new forms of collaboration and infrastructure are needed when technological change moves faster than any one institution can respond?Bio: Liat Krawczyk is the inaugural executive director of the New Jersey AI Hub, a public-private initiative launched by Princeton University, the State of New Jersey, Microsoft, and CoreWeave to advance AI innovation, adoption, and workforce development.Previously, she served at the U.S. Department of Commerce’s CHIPS Program Office, where she led workforce strategy and child care efforts tied to the nation’s historic investment in semiconductor manufacturing. Earlier, she led innovation initiatives at the New York City Economic Development Corporation, including work spanning cybersecurity, emerging technology, and the care economy, and has built and advised organizations at the intersection of technology, economic development, and public policy.Her work focuses on a central question of technological change: how institutions, industries, and communities can adapt quickly enough to turn innovation into broadly shared economic opportunity.This talk will be livestreamed and recorded.
